grammarPoints.title: 이에요/예요
grammarPoints.description: Attaches to a noun to mean "is/am/are" in polite informal speech. Use 이에요 after a noun ending in a consonant (받침), 예요 after a noun ending in a vowel.

notes.title: Consonant vs Vowel
notes.content: Use 이에요 after consonant-ending nouns (학생이에요) and 예요 after vowel-ending nouns (의사예요).

notes.title: Contracted Form
notes.content: In fast speech, 이에요 is sometimes shortened to 이예요, but the standard spelling is 이에요.

lessonExamples.notes: 책 ends in ㄱ, so use 이에요. Compare 의자예요, where 의자 ends in a vowel. For “is not,” learn the separate form 아니에요.

cards.englishHint: That over there is a book.

grammarPoints.title: 이다
grammarPoints.description: The dictionary/plain form of the copula "to be." Attaches directly to a noun. Used in writing, dictionary entries, and plain speech. Conjugates to 이에요/예요 (polite informal) and -입니다 (formal).

notes.title: Base Form
notes.content: 이다 is the base form you'll find in dictionaries. In conversation, use its conjugated forms (이에요/예요 or 입니다).

notes.title: No Space
notes.content: 이다 attaches directly to the noun with no space: 학생이다, not 학생 이다.

grammarPoints.title: 은/는
grammarPoints.description: Marks the topic of the sentence — "As for X…". Use 은 after a noun ending in a consonant (받침), 는 after a noun ending in a vowel. Often sets contrast or introduces a known topic.

notes.title: Consonant vs Vowel
notes.content: Use 은 after consonant-ending nouns (이름은) and 는 after vowel-ending nouns (저는).

notes.title: Topic vs Subject
notes.content: The topic particle marks "what we're talking about." The subject particle 이/가 (Lesson 2) marks "who/what does the action." They overlap but aren't the same.

lessonExamples.englishHint: As for me, I am a student.
lessonExamples.notes: Uses 이에요/예요 (GP1). 저 ends in vowel → 는.

lessonExamples.englishHint: As for the name, it's Minsu.
lessonExamples.notes: Uses 예요 (GP1). 이름 ends in consonant ㅁ → 은.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I drink coffee. As for tea, I don’t drink it.
lessonExamples.notes: 는 contrasts coffee with tea. The contrast comes from the two sentences together.

cards.englishHint: I rest on Saturdays. On Sundays I work. Make Saturday the contrasting topic.

grammarPoints.title: 이것
grammarPoints.description: A demonstrative pronoun meaning "this (thing)" — refers to something near the speaker. Often shortened to 이거 in casual speech. Part of a three-way system: 이것 (near me), 그것 (near you), 저것 (over there).

notes.title: Casual Form
notes.content: 이것 → 이거 in casual speech. Both are correct.

notes.title: Three-Way System
notes.content: Korean has three demonstratives based on distance: 이 (near speaker), 그 (near listener), 저 (far from both).

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3), 이에요/예요 (GP1).

grammarPoints.title: 그것
grammarPoints.description: A demonstrative pronoun meaning "that (thing)" — refers to something near the listener or something already mentioned. Often shortened to 그거 in casual speech.

notes.title: Casual Form
notes.content: 그것 → 그거 in casual speech.

notes.title: Referencing Earlier Topics
notes.content: 그것 can also refer to something previously mentioned in conversation, like English "that" or "it."

grammarPoints.title: 저것
grammarPoints.description: A demonstrative pronoun meaning "that (thing) over there" — refers to something far from both the speaker and listener. Often shortened to 저거 in casual speech.

notes.title: Casual Form
notes.content: 저것 → 저거 in casual speech.

notes.title: Don't Confuse
notes.content: 저것 (that over there) is different from 저 (I, humble). Context makes it clear.

lessonExamples.englishHint: That over there is a school.
That over there is a mountain.

cards.englishHint: That over there is a school.
That over there is a hospital.

grammarPoints.title: 의
grammarPoints.description: Connects two nouns to show possession, like English "'s" or "of." 저의 책 = "my book", 한국의 음식 = "Korean food." In casual speech, 저의 is often shortened to 제, and 나의 to 내.

notes.title: Pronunciation
notes.content: Though written 의, it is often pronounced 에 in casual speech.

notes.title: Contractions
notes.content: 저의 → 제 (my, polite), 나의 → 내 (my, casual). These contracted forms are very common.

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3), 예요 (GP1).
Uses 이것 (GP4), 은/는 (GP3), 이에요 (GP1).

grammarPoints.title: 도
grammarPoints.description: Replaces 은/는 or 이/가 to add the meaning "also" or "too." Attaches directly after the noun: 저도 = "me too." Does not change form — always 도 regardless of the preceding syllable.

notes.title: Replaces Other Particles
notes.content: 도 replaces 은/는, 이/가, or 을/를 — don't stack them (✗ 저는도, ✓ 저도).

notes.title: Position Matters
notes.content: 도 attaches to the noun it modifies: 저도 학생이에요 = "I am also a student" (emphasis on "I"), 학생도 = "a student too."

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 이에요 (GP1). N+1 OK: only uses GPs 1–8.
Uses 이것 (GP4), 의 (GP7), 이에요 (GP1).

grammarPoints.title: 이/가
grammarPoints.description: Marks the grammatical subject of a sentence. Use 이 after a noun ending in a consonant (받침), 가 after a noun ending in a vowel. Often used for new information or to answer "who/what."

notes.title: Consonant vs Vowel
notes.content: Use 이 after consonant-ending nouns (물이) and 가 after vowel-ending nouns (날씨가).

notes.title: Subject vs Topic
notes.content: 이/가 marks new or emphasized information ("Who came?" → 민수가 왔어요). 은/는 marks the general topic ("As for Minsu, he came").

lessonExamples.notes: 날씨 ends in vowel → 가. Uses vocab 좋아요 (good).
물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 이.
가 identifies the person who came. 누가 means “who” as the subject.

cards.englishHint: Who called? The teacher called. Identify who did it.

grammarPoints.title: 을/를
grammarPoints.description: Marks the direct object of a verb — what the action is done to. Use 을 after a noun ending in a consonant, 를 after a noun ending in a vowel.

notes.title: Consonant vs Vowel
notes.content: Use 을 after consonant-ending nouns (음악을) and 를 after vowel-ending nouns (커피를).

lessonExamples.notes: 커피 ends in vowel → 를.
책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을.

grammarPoints.title: -아요/어요
grammarPoints.description: The most common verb ending in everyday polite Korean. Attach to verb stems: -아요 when the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, -어요 for all other vowels. 하다 verbs become 해요. Expresses present actions, habits, and general truths.

notes.title: Vowel Harmony
notes.content: If the last vowel of the stem is ㅏ or ㅗ → 아요. Otherwise → 어요. 하다 → 해요 (special).

notes.title: Examples
notes.content: 가다 → 가요 (go), 먹다 → 먹어요 (eat), 공부하다 → 공부해요 (study).

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3), 을/를 (GP10). 공부하다 → 공부해요.
Uses 은/는 (GP3), 을/를 (GP10). 먹다 → 먹어요 (stem 먹 has ㅓ vowel).
가다 → 가요 (stem 가 has ㅏ vowel → 아요 contracts to 가요).
보다 → 봐요. The stem 보 and 아 combine to make 봐.

grammarPoints.title: 안
grammarPoints.description: Placed directly before a verb to negate it: "안 + verb" means "not verb." The simplest and most common way to negate in spoken Korean. For 하다 verbs, it goes between the noun and 하다: 공부 안 해요.

notes.title: 하다 Verbs
notes.content: For noun+하다 verbs, 안 goes between: 공부 안 해요 (not: 안 공부해요).

notes.title: 안 vs -지 않다
notes.content: 안 is the short form. The long form -지 않다 is taught later and used in formal/written contexts.

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3), 을/를 (GP10), -아요/어요 (GP11).
Uses 은/는 (GP3), -아요/어요 (GP11). 하다 verb split: 공부 안 해요.

cards.englishHint: Today I don’t drink coffee. Use the short negative form.

grammarPoints.title: 하고
grammarPoints.description: Connects two nouns meaning "and" or "with." Used in everyday speech after any noun regardless of ending. 친구하고 같이 = "together with a friend", 빵하고 우유 = "bread and milk."

notes.title: Formal Alternatives
notes.content: More formal/written: 과 (after consonant) / 와 (after vowel). Casual alternative: (이)랑.

notes.title: No Allomorphs
notes.content: 하고 doesn't change form — it's always 하고 regardless of the preceding syllable.

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 을/를 (GP10), -아요/어요 (GP11).
Uses -아요/어요 (GP11).

cards.englishHint: Please give me coffee and cake.

grammarPoints.title: 여기
grammarPoints.description: Means "here" — a place near the speaker. Part of a three-way system: 여기 (here, near me), 거기 (there, near you), 저기 (over there). Can take particles: 여기에 (at here), 여기는 (as for here).

notes.title: Three-Way Places
notes.content: 여기/거기/저기 follow the same 이/그/저 pattern as 이것/그것/저것.

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3), 예요 (GP1).

cards.englishHint: I put the book here, next to me.

grammarPoints.title: 거기
grammarPoints.description: Means "there" — a place near the listener or a previously mentioned place. Part of the 여기/거기/저기 system.

notes.title: Reference
notes.content: 거기 can also refer to a place already mentioned in the conversation, similar to English "there" or "that place."

cards.englishHint: What is there where you are?

grammarPoints.title: 저기
grammarPoints.description: Means "over there" — a place far from both the speaker and listener. Also used to get someone's attention: 저기요! = "Excuse me!"

notes.title: Attention Getter
notes.content: 저기요! is a common way to get a stranger's attention, like "Excuse me!" at a restaurant.

cards.englishHint: Over there is also a restaurant.
There is a bank over there away from both of us.

grammarPoints.title: -네요
grammarPoints.description: A sentence-ending expressing mild surprise or a new realization. Attaches to verb/adjective stems: 크다 → 크네요 ("Oh, it's big!"), 맛있다 → 맛있네요. Shows the speaker is noticing something for the first time.

notes.title: Direct Attachment
notes.content: -네요 attaches directly to the verb stem with no modification: 먹다 → 먹네요, 크다 → 크네요.

notes.title: Feeling
notes.content: -네요 conveys "Oh, I see!" or "Oh, how nice!" — a warm, observational tone.

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 이/가 (GP9). Stem 좋 + 네요.
Uses 이것 (GP4), 은/는 (GP3). Stem 맛있 + 네요.

grammarPoints.title: -지요/죠
grammarPoints.description: A sentence-ending that seeks confirmation or states something assumed to be common knowledge. 죠 is the contracted form of 지요 and is more common in speech. Equivalent to English "…right?" or "…isn't it?"

notes.title: Contraction
notes.content: 지요 → 죠 in casual speech. Both are polite. 죠 is overwhelmingly more common in conversation.

notes.title: Usage
notes.content: Use when you believe the listener already knows or agrees: "한국 음식 좋아하죠?" = "You like Korean food, right?"

lessonExamples.notes: Uses 은/는 (GP3). Stem 재미있 + 지요.
Uses 이것 (GP4), 은/는 (GP3). Contracted form 죠.

grammarPoints.title: 에 (장소)
grammarPoints.description: Marks a location or destination. Used with: (1) existence verbs (있다/없다): 집에 있어요 "I'm at home"; (2) movement verbs (가다/오다): 학교에 가요 "I go to school." Does not change form.

notes.title: 에 vs 에서
notes.content: 에 marks destination or static location (with 있다). 에서 marks where an action happens (with action verbs like 공부하다).

notes.title: Two Uses
notes.content: Destination: 학교에 가요 (go to school). Static location: 집에 있어요 (am at home).

lessonExamples.notes: The library is the destination. Compare 도서관에서 공부해요, where the library is the place of the action.
있어요 tells you where someone or something is.

grammarPoints.title: 있다/있어요
grammarPoints.description: Means "to exist" or "to have." Plain form: 있다. Polite: 있어요. Used for: (1) existence — 고양이가 있어요 "There is a cat"; (2) possession — 시간이 있어요 "I have time"; (3) location — 집에 있어요 "I am at home."

notes.title: Three Meanings
notes.content: Existence: 의자가 있어요 (there is a chair). Possession: 돈이 있어요 (I have money). Location: 여기에 있어요 (I am here).

notes.title: Subject Particle
notes.content: 이/가 introduces what exists: 고양이가 있어요 (there is a cat). 은/는 is possible when making it the topic or contrasting it: 고양이는 있어요 (as for a cat, there is one).

cards.englishHint: The book is on the desk.
There is a book in the bag.

grammarPoints.title: 없다/없어요
grammarPoints.hint: to not exist, to not have
grammarPoints.description: The negative counterpart of 있다. Means "to not exist" or "to not have." Plain form: 없다. Polite: 없어요. 돈이 없어요 "I don't have money"; 사람이 없어요 "There is no one."

notes.title: Pair with 있다
notes.content: 있다 (have/exist) ↔ 없다 (don't have / doesn't exist). They are a pair, not verb + negation.

notes.title: Not 안 있다
notes.content: For absence or lack of possession, use 없어요: 돈이 없어요 (I don’t have money). Learn it as the usual opposite of 있어요 in these examples.

grammarPoints.title: 에서
grammarPoints.description: Marks the location where an action takes place. Used with action verbs: 도서관에서 공부해요 "I study at the library." Contrast with 에, which marks destination or static location.

notes.title: 에서 vs 에
notes.content: Use 에서 for the location of an action (에서 공부해요 = study at). Use 에 for destination or static existence (에 가요 = go to, 에 있어요 = am at).

lessonExamples.englishHint: I drink coffee at the café.
I read a book at the library.
lessonExamples.notes: Reading is the action. The library tells you where it happens.

cards.englishHint: I drink coffee at the café.

grammarPoints.title: 위/아래/앞/뒤/옆
grammarPoints.description: Position nouns that combine with 에 to describe spatial relationships. Pattern: [Reference Noun] + 위/아래/앞/뒤/옆 + 에. 책상 위에 = "on the desk", 의자 아래에 = "under the chair."

notes.title: Five Position Words
notes.content: 위 (above/on), 아래 (below/under), 앞 (in front), 뒤 (behind), 옆 (beside/next to).

notes.title: Word Order
notes.content: Reference noun comes first, then the position: 책상 위에 = "desk above-at" = on the desk.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The book is on the desk.
The cat is under the chair.
There is a tree behind the house.
lessonExamples.notes: 집 뒤에 literally puts the house first, then “behind,” then the location particle.

cards.englishHint: The book is on the desk.
The cat is under the chair.
There is a store in front of the school.
There is a café next to the bank.
There is a park behind the school.

grammarPoints.title: 에 (시간)
grammarPoints.description: Marks a point in time: "at, on, in." 월요일에 = "on Monday", 3시에 = "at 3 o'clock", 아침에 = "in the morning." Same particle as location 에, but attached to time nouns.

notes.title: Not with 오늘/내일/어제
notes.content: 오늘, 내일, 어제, 지금 do NOT take 에 — they are already adverbs of time: ✗ 오늘에, ✓ 오늘.

notes.title: Shared Particle
notes.content: 에 serves both location and time. Context makes it clear.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I go to school at 9 o'clock.

grammarPoints.title: 부터
grammarPoints.description: Marks the starting point in time: "from" or "since." Often paired with 까지 (until): 9시부터 6시까지 = "from 9 to 6." Can also be used alone: 내일부터 = "starting from tomorrow."

notes.title: Often Paired
notes.content: 부터 often pairs with 까지: 부터~까지 = "from~until."

notes.title: Time Only
notes.content: 부터 is mainly used for time. For place "from," use 에서.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I study from Monday to Friday.

cards.englishHint: I have class from Monday to Friday.
I study from morning until evening.

grammarPoints.title: 까지
grammarPoints.description: Marks the ending point in time or space: "until" or "to." Often paired with 부터: 부터~까지 = "from~until." Can also mark extent: 여기까지 = "up to here."

notes.title: Time & Place
notes.content: 까지 works for both time (6시까지 "until 6") and place (서울까지 "to Seoul").

lessonExamples.englishHint: I study from morning until evening.

cards.englishHint: From Seoul to Busan it's far.

grammarPoints.title: 전에
grammarPoints.description: Means "before" a time or action. 수업 전에 = "before class." Can also follow a verb stem: 먹기 전에 = "before eating."

notes.title: Two Patterns
notes.content: With nouns: 수업 전에 (before class). With verbs: 먹기 전에 (before eating) — uses the -기 nominalizer.

cards.englishHint: I read a book before sleeping.

grammarPoints.title: 후에
grammarPoints.description: Means "after" a time or action. 수업 후에 = "after class." Can also follow a verb stem: 먹은 후에 = "after eating."

notes.title: Synonym
notes.content: 다음에 is a more casual alternative meaning "after" or "next time."

notes.title: Two Patterns
notes.content: With nouns: 수업 후에 (after class). With verbs: 먹은 후에 (after eating).

cards.englishHint: I meet a friend after work.
I take a walk after dinner.

grammarPoints.title: -았어요/-었어요
grammarPoints.description: The polite informal past tense ending. If the stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ → -았어요; otherwise → -었어요. 하다 verbs → 했어요. 가다 → 갔어요, 먹다 → 먹었어요, 공부하다 → 공부했어요.

notes.title: Vowel Harmony
notes.content: Last vowel ㅏ/ㅗ → 았어요. Other vowels → 었어요. 하다 → 했어요 (special).

notes.title: Contraction
notes.content: 가 + 았어요 → 갔어요, 보 + 았어요 → 봤어요, 마시 + 었어요 → 마셨어요. The vowels merge.

lessonExamples.notes: 보다 → 봤어요. 보 and 았 combine to make 봤.

grammarPoints.title: -지 않다
grammarPoints.description: The long-form negation pattern. Verb stem + 지 않다: 먹다 → 먹지 않아요 "do not eat." More formal/emphatic than the short 안 negation. Works with all verb types including 하다 verbs: 공부하지 않아요.

notes.title: 안 vs -지 않다
notes.content: 안 먹어요 and 먹지 않아요 mean the same thing. -지 않다 is slightly more formal or emphatic.

notes.title: 하다 Verbs
notes.content: For 하다 verbs, -지 않다 is simpler: 공부하지 않아요 (compare: 공부 안 해요).

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄴ
grammarPoints.description: Turns a descriptive verb (adjective) into a noun modifier. After a consonant stem → -은: 작다 → 작은. After a vowel stem → -ㄴ: 크다 → 큰. Compare 좋다 → 좋은 (regular), 길다 → 긴 (the stem-final ㄹ drops), and 빠르다 → 빠른.

notes.title: ㄹ-Irregular
notes.content: If the stem ends in ㄹ, drop ㄹ and add -ㄴ: 길다 → 긴, 멀다 → 먼.

notes.title: Action Verbs Differ
notes.content: Action verbs generally take -는 for present modification. They can take -(으)ㄴ for a completed action. Forms such as 있는 and 없는 also use -는.

cards.englishHint: I live in a small house.

grammarPoints.title: 만
grammarPoints.description: Attaches to a noun to mean "only" or "just." Replaces 은/는, 이/가, or 을/를 in most cases: 물만 마셔요 "I only drink water." Can stack with other particles: 에서만 "only at."

notes.title: Replaces Markers
notes.content: 만 typically replaces 은/는, 이/가, 을/를. 물을 마셔요 → 물만 마셔요.

notes.title: Stacking
notes.content: 만 can combine with location particles: 집에서만 (only at home), 학교에만 (only to school).

grammarPoints.title: -ㄴ 것 같다
grammarPoints.description: Expresses a guess or soft opinion about a present state. Descriptive verb stem + (으)ㄴ 것 같다: 비싼 것 같아요 "It seems expensive." For nouns: Noun + 인 것 같아요 "It seems to be [noun]."

notes.title: Soft Opinion
notes.content: Korean speakers often use -ㄴ 것 같다 for politeness even when they are sure, to soften the statement.

notes.title: Tense Matters
notes.content: For past: -ㄴ 것 같다 (same form for adj). For action verbs in present: -는 것 같다 (different ending, later lesson).

cards.fullSentence: 그 사람은 한국 사람인 것 같아요.
cards.englishHint: That person seems to be Korean.

grammarPoints.title: -고 싶다
grammarPoints.description: Expresses a desire or wish. Verb stem + 고 싶다: 먹다 → 먹고 싶어요 "I want to eat." Past form: -고 싶었어요 "I wanted to." Use it to express your own desire or ask the listener what they want. To describe someone else’s visible desire, the usual form is -고 싶어하다.

notes.title: First/Second Person
notes.content: -고 싶다 is for "I want" or "Do you want?" For third person desires, use -고 싶어하다.

notes.title: No Conjugation Needed
notes.content: The verb stem stays unchanged: 가다 → 가고 싶어요, 먹다 → 먹고 싶어요. No vowel harmony rules.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I want to go to Korea.

cards.englishHint: I want to go to Korea.
I want to watch a movie.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다
grammarPoints.hint: can, able to / cannot, unable to
grammarPoints.description: Expresses ability or possibility. Verb stem + (으)ㄹ 수 있다: 먹을 수 있어요 "can eat." Negative: -(으)ㄹ 수 없다: 먹을 수 없어요 "cannot eat." After consonant stem → -을 수 있다; after vowel stem → -ㄹ 수 있다.

notes.title: Allomorphs
notes.content: Consonant stem: 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. Vowel stem: 가다 → 갈 수 있어요. ㄹ stem: 만들다 → 만들 수 있어요 (ㄹ stays).

notes.title: 있다 vs 없다
notes.content: 수 있다 = can/able. 수 없다 = cannot/unable. Both conjugate normally: 있어요/없어요.

lessonExamples.notes: 없어요 gives the negative meaning. 수 is separated from the verb by a space.

cards.englishHint: I can’t go today. Use the 수 pattern.

grammarPoints.title: 못
grammarPoints.description: Short-form inability negation. Placed before the verb: 못 먹어요 "cannot eat." For 하다 verbs, 못 goes between the noun and 하다: 운동 못 해요. Indicates inability (cannot), not refusal (won't). Compare with 안 (choice not to).

notes.title: 못 vs 안
notes.content: 못 = cannot (inability/impossibility). 안 = do not (choice/preference). 못 먹어요 (can't eat) vs 안 먹어요 (don't eat).

notes.title: 하다 Split
notes.content: For Noun+하다 verbs: 공부 못 해요 (cannot study), not 못 공부해요.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어야 하다
grammarPoints.description: Expresses obligation or necessity. Verb stem + 아야/어야 하다: 가다 → 가야 해요 "must go." 먹다 → 먹어야 해요 "must eat." 하다 → 해야 해요 "must do." Same vowel harmony as -아요/어요.

notes.title: Vowel Harmony
notes.content: Same as -아요/어요: stem ㅏ/ㅗ → 아야 해요; otherwise → 어야 해요. 하다 → 해야 해요.

notes.title: Negative
notes.content: -지 않아도 돼요 means "don't have to" (no obligation). Not covered here but useful to know.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I have to go to school tomorrow.

cards.englishHint: I have to go to school tomorrow.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)세요
grammarPoints.description: Polite imperative form used for requests and instructions. After consonant stem → -으세요: 읽다 → 읽으세요. After vowel stem → -세요: 가다 → 가세요. Also used as honorific present: 어머니가 가세요 "Mother goes/is going."

notes.title: Dual Use
notes.content: -(으)세요 is both a polite imperative ("please do") and an honorific form. Context determines meaning.

notes.title: Irregular
notes.content: ㄹ-ending stems drop ㄹ: 만들다 → 만드세요. 듣다 → 들으세요 (ㄷ-irregular).

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 주세요
grammarPoints.description: Polite request asking someone to do something as a favor. Verb stem + 아/어 주세요: 가르치다 → 가르쳐 주세요 "please teach me." Same vowel harmony as -아요/어요. More specifically requesting action for the speaker's benefit.

notes.title: -(으)세요 vs -아/어 주세요
notes.content: -(으)세요 is a general polite command. -아/어 주세요 specifically asks "please do this for me" — implies a favor.

notes.title: Common Phrases
notes.content: 도와주세요 (please help), 알려 주세요 (please let me know), 기다려 주세요 (please wait).

grammarPoints.title: -아/어서
grammarPoints.description: Connects two clauses where the first is the reason for the second. Verb stem + 아서/어서: 배가 고파서 밥을 먹었어요 "Because I was hungry, I ate." Same vowel harmony as -아요/어요. In the pattern taught here, put tense on the final verb.

notes.title: Where to put tense
notes.content: For these beginner examples, leave the reason clause unmarked for tense and mark the main verb. Compare -(으)니까 when explicitly marking a past reason.

notes.title: Common Combinations
notes.content: 만나서 반갑습니다 (Nice to meet you — lit. "meeting, I am pleased"). 늦어서 죄송합니다 (Sorry for being late).

lessonExamples.englishHint: I ate because I was hungry.
I stayed home because I was tired.

cards.englishHint: I ate because I was hungry.
I took an umbrella because it was raining.
I took a taxi because I was late.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)니까
grammarPoints.description: Connects a reason clause to a result clause. More subjective than -아/어서. After consonant stem → -으니까: 읽다 → 읽으니까. After vowel stem → -니까: 가다 → 가니까. CAN take past tense: 갔으니까. Often used with commands/suggestions.

notes.title: -(으)니까 vs -아/어서
notes.content: -(으)니까 is more subjective and can precede commands: 시간이 없으니까 빨리 가세요. Use -(으)니까 for a reason followed by a command or suggestion in this lesson.

notes.title: Past OK
notes.content: -(으)니까 allows past tense: 이미 먹었으니까 안 먹어요 (I already ate, so I'm not eating).

lessonExamples.englishHint: Please go quickly because there's no time.
Please dress warmly because it's cold.

cards.englishHint: Please go quickly because there's no time.
Take an umbrella because it's raining.
Please eat a lot because it's delicious.

grammarPoints.title: 그래서
grammarPoints.description: Sentence-initial connector meaning "so" or "therefore." Links two sentences where the first is the cause: 비가 왔어요. 그래서 집에 있었어요. "It rained. So I stayed home." Can also be used as a question: 그래서요? "So (what happened)?"

notes.title: Sentence Connector
notes.content: 그래서 connects two independent sentences. Unlike -아/어서 and -(으)니까, it doesn't connect clauses within one sentence.

notes.title: Related Words
notes.content: 그래서 (so/therefore), 그런데 (but/however), 그리고 (and/also) are the three most common sentence connectors.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I was hungry. So I ate.
It rained. So I stayed home.

cards.englishHint: I was hungry. So I ate.
I had no time. So I took a taxi.
I like Korean. So I study every day.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)면
grammarPoints.description: Conditional connector meaning "if" or "when." After consonant stem → -으면: 먹다 → 먹으면. After vowel stem → -면: 가다 → 가면. 시간이 있으면 같이 가요 "If you have time, let's go together."

notes.title: Hypothetical & Habitual
notes.content: -(으)면 covers both hypothetical (if it rains) and habitual (whenever I eat). Context determines which.

notes.title: ㄹ-Irregular
notes.content: Stems ending in ㄹ: drop ㄹ, add -면. 살다 → 살면, 알다 → 알면.

lessonExamples.englishHint: If you have time, let's go together.
If it rains, I stay home.

cards.englishHint: If you have time, let's go together.
If I go to Korea, I want to eat bulgogi.
If the weather is nice, I go to the park.

grammarPoints.title: -지만
grammarPoints.description: Clause-level contrast connector. Verb/Adj stem + 지만: 비싸지만 맛있어요 "It's expensive but delicious." Can also take tense: 갔지만 "went but." Always attaches directly to the stem (no vowel harmony).

notes.title: No Vowel Harmony
notes.content: -지만 attaches directly to any stem. No consonant/vowel distinction. 먹다 → 먹지만, 가다 → 가지만.

notes.title: With Tense
notes.content: Past: 갔지만, 먹었지만. The tense goes between the stem and -지만.

cards.englishHint: I'm tired but I have to study.
It's small but a nice house.

grammarPoints.title: 하지만
grammarPoints.description: Sentence-initial contrast connector meaning "but" or "however." Links two sentences: 한국어는 어려워요. 하지만 재미있어요. "Korean is hard. But it's fun." Compare with -지만 which connects clauses within one sentence.

notes.title: -지만 vs 하지만
notes.content: -지만 connects clauses within one sentence. 하지만 connects two separate sentences. Same meaning, different scope.

notes.title: Similar Words
notes.content: 하지만, 그런데, 그렇지만 all mean "but/however." 하지만 is the most common in writing.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Korean is hard. But it's fun.
It rained. But I went to the park.

cards.englishHint: Korean is hard. But it's fun.
That restaurant is expensive. But it's delicious.
I'm tired. But I have to study.

grammarPoints.title: -고
grammarPoints.description: Connects two actions sequentially or lists parallel actions. Verb stem + 고: 밥을 먹고 커피를 마셔요 "I eat and (then) drink coffee." No vowel harmony — always 고. Can express time order or simple listing.

notes.title: No Conjugation
notes.content: -고 attaches directly to any verb stem. No consonant/vowel rules: 먹고, 가고, 하고. Same form as 하고 (and/with) for nouns.

notes.title: Order Matters
notes.content: When sequential: 손을 씻고 밥을 먹어요 (wash hands THEN eat). When listing: 노래하고 춤을 춰요 (sing AND dance — simultaneous).

lessonExamples.englishHint: I eat breakfast and then go to school.
I do homework and then watch TV.

cards.englishHint: I eat breakfast and then go to school.
I showered and then got dressed.
I drink coffee and then start work.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ게요
grammarPoints.description: Expresses the speaker's intention or promise, with consideration for the listener. After consonant stem → -을게요: 먹다 → 먹을게요. After vowel stem → -ㄹ게요: 가다 → 갈게요. First person only. Implies "I will (and you should know / it affects you)."

notes.title: First Person Only
notes.content: -(으)ㄹ게요 is ONLY for "I will." For "you/he/she will," use -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

notes.title: vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요
notes.content: -(으)ㄹ게요 = promise/consideration for listener. -(으)ㄹ 거예요 = plan/prediction (any person).

lessonExamples.englishHint: Is your bag heavy? I’ll carry it for you.
lessonExamples.notes: The speaker offers to do something for the listener.

cards.englishHint: Shall I open the door? I’ll open it. Make an offer to the listener.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ 거예요
grammarPoints.description: Expresses a future plan or prediction. Works for all persons. After consonant stem → -을 거예요: 먹다 → 먹을 거예요. After vowel stem → -ㄹ 거예요: 가다 → 갈 거예요. 내일 뭐 할 거예요? "What will you do tomorrow?"

notes.title: All Persons
notes.content: 저는 갈 거예요 (I will go). 친구는 갈 거예요 (My friend will go). 비가 올 거예요 (It will rain). Any subject works.

notes.title: Questions
notes.content: 뭐 할 거예요? (What will you do?), 어디 갈 거예요? (Where will you go?) — very common question patterns.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I'm going to study Korean tomorrow.
I'm going to meet a friend on the weekend.

cards.englishHint: I'm going to study Korean tomorrow.
What are you going to eat tonight?
I'm going to go to Korea next year.
